generatedBy: SI drafted from each PSI record's objective, approach and research impacts fields. To be checked against PSI data by the team.

PSI-10.burned: Ethylene and methane gas flames around a small spherical burner, in both normal and inverse (inside-out) form.
PSI-10.varied: Oxygen level, dilution with inert gas, flow rate and pressure.
PSI-10.matters: It maps when gas flames make soot and when they go out, which feeds the flame models that fire safety tools rely on.

PSI-20.burned: Methane and ethylene gas mixtures fed through porous flat burners of 25 and 50 mm, standing in for burning solids and liquids.
PSI-20.varied: The surrounding oxygen level, the burner size and the fuel mixture.
PSI-20.matters: The record says burning like that of materials such as PMMA and Nylon carried on in microgravity with no air flow, which matters because stopping ventilation is a standard step in fighting a spacecraft fire.

PSI-21.burned: Methane and ethylene gas flames in a slow stream of air around the burner (coflow).
PSI-21.varied: Flow speed and how much the fuel was diluted.
PSI-21.matters: It gives clean data on weak and sooty flames to test computer models of flame shape, lift-off and extinction.

PSI-22.burned: Methane and ethylene gas flames between a burner and a charged mesh.
PSI-22.varied: The electric field, its polarity and the fuel concentration.
PSI-22.matters: It shows how an electric field pulls on flame ions and moves a flame. The challenge statement notes this was used to mimic partial gravity.

PSI-23.burned: Hydrogen, methane and ethylene mixtures from a spherical porous burner, giving round flames.
PSI-23.varied: The fuel mixture, the inert gas and the oxygen level, near 21 and 30 percent.
PSI-23.matters: Simple round flames let models of flame structure and extinction be tested without buoyancy in the way.

PSI-25.burned: Solid samples such as PMMA rods, PMMA films and fabric in a small wind tunnel in the glovebox.
PSI-25.varied: Oxygen level, air flow speed, flow direction and sample thickness.
PSI-25.matters: It measures where a solid stops burning in low flow, to connect NASA's ground flammability test with how materials really burn in microgravity.

PSI-26.burned: Solid samples including cotton and fiberglass fabric, Nomex and PMMA spheres in a small wind tunnel in the glovebox.
PSI-26.varied: Material, sample shape and air flow. Some tests used nitrogen to put the flame out.
PSI-26.matters: It begins to bridge NASA's normal gravity screening test (NASA-STD-6001 Test 1) and real flammability in microgravity.

PSI-39.burned: Droplets of n-dodecane and mixtures with iso-dodecane, some held on a fiber.
PSI-39.varied: Pressure, oxygen level and helium dilution.
PSI-39.matters: It studies cool flames, where a droplet keeps burning at low temperature after the visible flame goes out.

PSI-47.burned: Nothing was burned. It sampled dust and aerosol particles in ISS cabin air.
PSI-47.varied: The instrument used and the place sampled.
PSI-47.matters: It proved a particle counter could work in microgravity before the SAME smoke experiment relied on it, which supports better smoke detectors.

PSI-60.burned: Nothing new was burned. This ground study analysed images of SPICE gas jet flames held in PSI.
PSI-60.varied: The analysis compared soot in normal gravity and microgravity flames.
PSI-60.matters: It turns archived flame images into soot temperature and soot amount, which improves models of soot and heat from flames.

PSI-62.burned: Nothing new was burned. This ground study modelled flame spread over solids and compared it with BASS flight data.
PSI-62.varied: The modelling method, checked against flames spreading with the air flow.
PSI-62.matters: The record says it provides predictive tools for screening the flammability limits of new materials.

PSI-68.burned: Droplets of liquid fuels such as heptane, octane, decane and alcohol mixtures.
PSI-68.varied: Fuel, oxygen level, pressure, the inert gas and flow speed.
PSI-68.matters: It extends FLEX to more realistic fuels and gives benchmark data to test models of droplet burning and extinction.

PSI-69.burned: Single droplets of methanol and heptane, a few millimetres across.
PSI-69.varied: Oxygen level, pressure and the added gases carbon dioxide and helium.
PSI-69.matters: It maps where liquid fuel flames go out in microgravity and how well gaseous suppressants work, which informs extinguisher design.

PSI-98.burned: A large sheet of cotton and fiberglass fabric, about 40 cm wide and 94 cm long, inside an uncrewed Cygnus cargo vehicle.
PSI-98.varied: The direction of the air flow relative to the flame.
PSI-98.matters: It shows how fast a large fire grows in low gravity, at a scale that cannot be tested with a crew aboard.

PSI-99.burned: Nine smaller samples including silicone, cotton and fiberglass fabric, PMMA and Nomex, inside an uncrewed Cygnus cargo vehicle.
PSI-99.varied: Material, thickness and flow direction, with the same samples also tested in normal gravity.
PSI-99.matters: It compares low gravity flammability limits with NASA's normal gravity screening test, material by material.

PSI-100.burned: A large sheet of cotton and fiberglass fabric inside an uncrewed Cygnus cargo vehicle, at a higher air flow than Saffire-I.
PSI-100.varied: The direction of the air flow relative to the flame.
PSI-100.matters: It adds a second large scale fire test in low gravity, to see how flow speed changes fire growth.

PSI-101.burned: Nothing was set alight. Samples of Kapton, silicone, lamp wick, Pyrell and Teflon were overheated to make smoke.
PSI-101.varied: Material, air flow, heating and how long the smoke aged before it was measured.
PSI-101.matters: It measures smoke particle sizes in microgravity so that future spacecraft fire detectors can be tuned to real smoke.

PSI-102.burned: Nothing was set alight. Spacecraft materials such as Teflon were overheated to make smoke.
PSI-102.varied: Material, air flow and smoke ageing time.
PSI-102.matters: The record says SAME will provide technology for an advanced fire detector for long missions.

PSI-106.burned: Methane, ethylene and nitrogen-diluted gas jet flames in the glovebox flow duct.
PSI-106.varied: Fuel, dilution, burner size and flow speed.
PSI-106.matters: It studies what holds a flame to its burner and when it lifts off, which improves models of flame stability.

PSI-107.burned: Gas jet flames of methane, ethylene, propane and propylene in a stream of air.
PSI-107.varied: Fuel, nozzle size, fuel flow and air speed.
PSI-107.matters: It finds the smoke point, the flame size at which a flame starts to give off soot, with no buoyancy.

PSI-115.burned: Nothing was burned. This ground study simulated smoke particles from the SAME experiment.
PSI-115.varied: Gravity level in the simulation, Earth gravity against microgravity.
PSI-115.matters: The record says such models would lead to better smoke detection devices.

PSI-117.burned: Nothing was burned. This ground study simulated cool flames on fuel droplets using FLEX flight data.
PSI-117.varied: Heating and drift of the droplet in the simulation.
PSI-117.matters: It explains why cool flames behaved differently from run to run, which improves spacecraft fire models.

PSI-142.burned: Laboratory flames on the ground, set up to mirror FLEX conditions.
PSI-142.varied: Oxygen level and the addition of ozone.
PSI-142.matters: It maps when cool flames can exist and when they go out, building on FLEX data.

PSI-159.burned: Gas flames of ethane, propane, butane and similar fuels around a spherical burner, in normal and inverse form.
PSI-159.varied: Fuel, oxygen level up to 85 percent in the oxidizer stream, dilution and pressure.
PSI-159.matters: It finds the conditions where cool gas flames exist, and holds the highest oxygen levels of any microgravity test in PSI.
